title: Italy PM Meloni seeks EU trademark for her voice amid AI deepfake risks
source_used: Reuters wire text as carried by The Straits Times (Reuters page itself returns 401); cross-checked with Euronews Italia (citing la Repubblica) and EU Today
key_facts: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has applied to the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) to trademark her voice, to protect herself against AI-generated deepfakes; records showed this on 5 Oct 2026.
The application, dated 5 Oct on the EUIPO website and confirmed by her office, includes a four-second audio recording of herself twice repeating, in Italian, 'I am Giorgia Meloni'.
'Io Sono Giorgia' (I Am Giorgia) was the title of her 2021 autobiography; it echoed a declaration she made at a political rally in 2019 and was turned into a disco track.

Manipulated images of Meloni have circulated online in recent years and at times been shared as authentic; she has denounced such material, urged users to verify content before sharing, and said that while she can defend herself, many others cannot.

Italian media have reported that even if approved, the application would not by itself prevent the use of her voice in AI-generated deepfakes, though it could create additional legal obstacles for those seeking to replicate it.
In 2024 Meloni launched a civil action against a man from Sardinia accused of creating and posting deepfake pornographic images using her face; the case is still pending before an Italian court.
quote_evidence: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has applied to the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) to trademark her voice in a new move to protect herself against AI-generated deepfakes, records showed on Oct 5.
Her application, dated Oct 5 on the EUIPO website and confirmed by her office, includes a four-second audio recording of herself twice repeating the phrase, in Italian, “I am Giorgia Meloni”.

Italian media have reported that even if approved, the application would not by itself prevent the use of her voice in AI-generated deepfakes, though it could create additional legal obstacles for those seeking to replicate it.
why_it_matters_hint: A head of government is testing trademark law as a legal obstacle against AI copies of her voice; the filing is not yet approved and would not by itself stop deepfakes.
notes: Reuters page returns 401, so read as the Reuters wire text on The Straits Times (ends REUTERS). Euronews Italia, citing la Repubblica (first to report it on Monday morning), says the application is 'under examination' and is handled by the Rome law firm MpmLegal; EU Today agrees. Singer Giusy Ferreri and voice actor Luca Ward have filed similar voice marks (Euronews). Reuters does not name the Italian media it cites.
